semantic_reviews.coverage_confirmed: items_read: All 29 records in items_5.json: 24 single items (DEF, FEATURE, PROC, CHAIN, APP, SYNTH, MISCON) and three papers (P01: 12 MCQ, P02: 8 marks, P03: 10 marks). notes_read: Every section of topics/5/5-relationship-of-organisms-with-one-another-and-with-their-environment.md in full: 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4.1 and 5.4.2, including the key points and 'Where this connects' blocks. not_checked: No flashcards beyond the single items listed in the file. Figures VIS-6116-* were not checked (held, so only the wording was judged). AO, Bloom, command-word and tariff labels were not checked, as excluded by the brief. Deterministic checks were not re-run. Topics other than 5 were not checked, and the depth of cross-referenced content in other topics was not verified.
semantic_reviews.reconstruction_test: q6_learner_test: OBJ-6116-5.2-01 (ITEM-6116-5-020-MECH, 4 marks): from the notes alone a learner can write fixation, uptake of nitrate and feeding, decomposition to ammonium, nitrification with oxygen, and denitrification in waterlogged soil, which earns 4/4. OBJ-6116-5.4.2-17 (ITEM-6116-5-105-SYNTH, 5 marks): 'Investigating poaching and tourism' supplies the matched periods and sites, the tourism measures, season and road-closure confounders, anonymised authorised records, a table repeated over periods, and a conclusion that does not claim proof. The notes never use the words independent or dependent variable, but they name both quantities, so the answer would probably earn 4-5/5. Six sampled single items (004, 023, 025, 030, 050, 064) can each be answered from the notes alone. q7_misconceptions: Only ITEM-6116-5-108-MISCON carries a misconception_entry (MISCON-6116-033). It checks recall but does not discriminate, and its stem signals that the idea is wrong (finding 5-009). P01 Q1 discriminates the same misconception through its decomposer distractors.

issues.finding: The worked example sets a condition of fewer than 40 visitors a day for successful breeding, then recommends a cap of 40, which allows exactly 40 visitors. At 40 visitors the stated condition is not met, so the recommended cap does not protect the birds by the example's own rule. Arithmetic (80 x 120 = N$9600; 40 x 120 = N$4800) is correct.
issues.educational_consequence: Learners copy an inclusive/exclusive boundary slip in threshold questions and apply a limit that sits on the failing side of the stated condition.
issues.recommended_repair: Change the condition to '40 or fewer visitors a day', or change the cap to 39 visitors (39 x 120 = N$4680).
issues.resolution: Tourism worked example condition changed to '40 or fewer visitors a day', so the cap of 40 (N$4800) satisfies it; consistent with item 5.4.2-15 APP ('falls when more than 40'). (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The canonical answer skips the algal growth and death step and never names decomposers or their respiration, yet marking point 1 requires 'growth and then death of algae and plants, so decomposers use more oxygen'. As written, the model answer would not earn its own first mark. It also jumps from nutrients straight to 'decay', which is the very missing-step error the notes warn about.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner who models their answer on the canonical text writes nutrients -> decay and loses the mechanism mark for omitting algal growth/death and decomposer respiration.
issues.recommended_repair: Rewrite the first sentence: 'Excess nutrients cause rapid growth of algae and plants; when they die, decomposers break down the dead material and their aerobic respiration uses up dissolved oxygen.'
issues.resolution: ITEM 5-087 canonical answer now gives rapid algal/plant growth, death, decomposer aerobic respiration using dissolved oxygen, matching mark 1. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The objective asks for the effects of cutting down forests on the balance between oxygen AND carbon dioxide. The notes section discusses only carbon dioxide and carbon stores; it never states that removing trees reduces the oxygen released by photosynthesis, or that burning cleared trees uses oxygen. The fossil-fuel section (5.2-12) does treat oxygen, so the omission is specific to forests.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner answering a 'balance between oxygen and carbon dioxide' question on deforestation omits the oxygen half and loses marks.
issues.recommended_repair: Add: 'Fewer trees means less photosynthesis, so less oxygen is released and less carbon dioxide removed; burning or decay of the felled trees uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. As with fossil fuels, the change in atmospheric oxygen is small compared with the change in carbon dioxide.'
issues.resolution: 5.2-13 notes add oxygen: less photosynthesis releases less oxygen and removes less CO2; burning/decay uses oxygen and releases CO2; oxygen change small relative to CO2. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The objective requires learners to identify the phases of a sigmoid curve and explain the role of limiting factors in each phase. The notes describe the phases only informally ('lag phase', 'phase of rapid increase', 'slowing phase', 'roughly stable phase') and never give the conventional names exponential (log) phase and stationary phase, nor mention a death/decline phase. The lag phase is not explained (only 'the population is small and growth is slow'), and the role of limiting factors in the lag and rapid phases (few limiting factors acting, plenty of resources) is not stated.
issues.educational_consequence: Learners asked to 'name phase X' on a curve may not produce 'exponential/log' or 'stationary', and cannot explain why the lag phase is slow or why limiting factors are weak in the exponential phase.
issues.recommended_repair: Name the phases lag, exponential (log), stationary (and optionally death), and give one limiting-factor explanation per phase: lag - few breeding individuals, still establishing; exponential - resources plentiful, limiting factors weak, births far exceed deaths; stationary - food, space, disease or predation limit growth so births roughly equal deaths. Check against the NSSCO/Cambridge marking convention before adding the death phase.
issues.resolution: 5.3-05 entry and notes name lag, exponential (log), stationary and death phases with a limiting-factor explanation for each (Cambridge 0610 convention includes death phase). (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The figures are correct (1000 -> 200 -> 40 -> 8 kJ at 20% per transfer; 200 and 40 exceed 30, 8 does not), but 'the first two levels can be supported but the third cannot' is ambiguous because the producer base is itself a trophic level. The intended meaning is that the primary and secondary consumer levels can be supported and the tertiary level cannot.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner counting the producers as level 1 concludes that only primary consumers are supported and miscounts the length of the chain.
issues.recommended_repair: Write 'the primary and secondary consumer levels (200 kJ and 40 kJ) can be supported but a tertiary consumer level (8 kJ) cannot'.
issues.resolution: Worked example now says primary and secondary consumer levels (200, 40 kJ) supported, tertiary (8 kJ) not. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The 5.1 key-points summary gives only egestion and respiration as the reasons less energy passes on at each step and drops uneaten material, which the body text includes. Mark schemes at this level usually credit 'not all of the organism is eaten'.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner revising from the summary alone gives two reasons and misses a creditable third (parts not eaten).
issues.recommended_repair: Key points: 'because some material is not eaten, some is egested, and much is used in respiration and lost as heat'.
issues.resolution: 5.1 key points give uneaten material, egestion, and respiration/heat loss. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The second mark requires stating that households' food at home runs out over several weeks, but the stem says nothing about household stocks. The stem also places the grain 'nearby', which weakens the claim that a closed road stops people reaching it.
issues.educational_consequence: Learners are rewarded for adding an unstated fact (empty home stores); a learner who notes that grain 'nearby' could be walked to is penalised for reading the stem carefully.
issues.recommended_repair: Revise the stem to 'grain is stored in a town 60 km away; households had about one week of food at home and the only road has been closed for five weeks'.
issues.resolution: ITEM 5-058 stem: grain in a town 60 km away, about one week of food at home, only road closed five weeks; answer and mark 2 aligned. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: Q6 asks which 'observation' would show extinction, but the key (B, 'None remains alive anywhere') is the definition of extinction, not something anyone can observe. The notes themselves stress that failing to find a species does not show it is extinct.
issues.educational_consequence: Learners may come to think extinction is something a survey can directly observe, which works against the effort-and-detection point taught in 5.4.2.
issues.recommended_repair: Reword the stem to 'Which statement describes a species that is extinct?'
issues.resolution: P01 Q6 stem reworded to 'Which statement describes a species that is extinct?'; options and key unchanged. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The item announces that the idea is wrong ('Explain the error'), so the learner never has to choose between producer and decomposer. The stated premise ('because it releases mineral ions') is also an unusual reason, not the common confusion the notes describe (an organism placed at the bottom of a diagram or at the start of a decay chain). The item checks recall of the distinction but does not discriminate the misconception. P01 Q1 does discriminate it, with fungus and bacterium distractors.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner holding the misconception can still score by stating the producer definition, so the item does not show whether the misconception has gone.
issues.recommended_repair: Ask the learner to classify a fungus on dead leaves and an alga on the same leaf litter, each with a reason, or base the premise on the observed confusion (a fungus at the start of a decay chain).
issues.resolution: ITEM 5-108 MISCON rewritten: fungus drawn first in a decay chain; learner P says producer, Q says decomposer; learner must choose and explain. Tariff, subtype, command word unchanged. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)
